Archaeologists discovered a stash of Celtic coins ahead of a construction project for an electrical substation in Hungary.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Hungary have discovered a stash of more than 200 Celtic silver coins that are over 2,000 years old. It's one of the largest hoards found there in decades.

Researchers unearthed the coins during excavations ahead of construction for an electrical substation in western Hungary between 2023 and 2025, according to a translated statement from the power company E.ON. The hoard dates to sometime between the late second century B.C. and the early first century B.C.

The coin cache weighs roughly 4.4 pounds (2 kilograms). In today's market, it's worth more than $2,000 as raw silver alone, but its rarity and historical value effectively make it priceless, the statement said.

The site was once part of a farm, and plowing there had unearthed several individual coins in recent decades, the statement said.

During the latest excavations, archaeologists initially found a few coins and then searched the area with metal detectors, which led them to the coin hoard. The treasure had been packed inside a small ceramic vessel and sat about 16 inches (40 centimeters) below ground.

"This is a rarity in Europe," Eszter Kreiter, an archaeologist at Hungary's National Archaeological Institute, said at a news conference, according to local news outlets. She added that the last similar find was made in Hungary in the late 1960s.

The hoard's silver coins are modeled on Greek tetradrachms — a very early type of large silver coin that was introduced in the late sixth century B.C.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The newfound Celtic tetradrachm copies are a type known as "Velem," which are named after Velem-Szent Vid, a fortified Celtic hilltop settlement, or oppidum. Similar coins have been found at that site, which is located about 10 miles (15 kilometers) to the west.

Each coin has a stylized head on one side that probably depicts the Greek god Apollo, and portrays a helmeted rider and horse on the other side.

Artifacts from more than 7,000 years of occupation have been found at the site, including a glass bead (bottom, center) thought to be about 2,500 years old.

The excavations have revealed evidence of more than 7,000 years of occupation at the site, officials wrote in the statement. The artifacts include a nearly 7,000-year-old polished stone chisel used for woodworking and a glass bead with a peacock's eye pattern that seems to have been part of jewelry from the sixth or seventh century B.C.

A Roman-era villa was built at the same site in later centuries, without disturbing the hoard of buried silver, Kreiter said at the news conference.

The site in Hungary's western Szombathely region was excavated between 2023 and 2025 ahead of the construction of an electricity substation.

The villa has long since been demolished, but the excavations enabled the archaeological team to reconstruct its floor plan, including its underfloor heating system, she said. They also found a Roman-era brick with a dog's paw print.

The artifacts from the site will become part of a museum exhibition.

According to Museum Wales, the Celts were loosely related Iron Age peoples descended from Proto-Indo-European speakers. Emerging in Central Europe, Celtic groups occupied much of Central and Western Europe from about the 10th to the first century B.C. The Celtic Gauls were finally defeated by the Romans, led by Julius Caesar at Alesia, now in eastern France, in 52 B.C. The Britons were also Celtic, though most people of Celtic descent would not have recognized that name.

Several modern ethnic groups, including the native Irish and the Bretons of coastal France, trace their descent to the Celts. Regions with strong Celtic origins are sometimes called the "Celtic fringe" of Western Europe.

Writing in the Journal of Roman Studies, the British coin expert Christopher Howgego, an honorary curator and professor emeritus of Greek and Roman numismatics at the University of Oxford, stated that Celtic tribes in the Carpathian Basin, now in Hungary and Romania, started minting their own silver coins after Celtic mercenaries had seen them when serving with Hellenistic armies in Greece and Macedonia.

Howgego has written that the Greek-inspired Celtic coins included adaptations of classical Greek portraits, as well as distinctive Celtic designs. These copycat tetradrachms held very high value for their makers, so they were rarely used for everyday purchases. Instead, they were often hoarded as wealth or buried as ritual offerings.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6299. Scientists Discover a Potential New Way To Treat Diabetes – No Insulin Required

A discovery in animal muscle suggests that the body’s natural ability to absorb sugar without insulin could be harnessed to develop new diabetes treatments.

For people with diabetes or insulin resistance, controlling blood sugar can be difficult because their muscles do not respond effectively to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells. Muscles, however, have another way of absorbing glucose that does not require insulin. Understanding how this process works could give researchers an entirely new way to treat high blood sugar.

Scientists at the University of Cincinnati (UC) College of Medicine have identified a previously unknown pathway that allows skeletal muscles to absorb glucose independently of insulin. Their findings, published in the Nature Portfolio journal Communications Biology, could provide a new target for treating diabetes, hyperglycemia, and insulin resistance.

Skeletal muscle makes up about 40% of the human body and plays a major role in regulating blood sugar. After a meal, rising insulin levels stimulate muscles to absorb and store up to 90% of ingested glucose through a transport protein called GLUT4, which helps glucose enter muscle cells.

During exercise or stress, insulin levels drop, yet working muscles can absorb glucose at rates up to 100 times higher than after a meal to meet the energy demands of contraction. How muscles manage this without insulin has remained a mystery despite decades of research.

To investigate, the researchers developed a way to measure glucose uptake independently of insulin. They used glucose derivatives that could be carried by a family of transport proteins known as SGLTs but not by GLUT4. The team tested these derivatives in isolated muscles from animal models, using electrical stimulation to reproduce the contractions of working muscles.

“We showed that if we stimulate muscle to contract in insulin-free conditions, it can take up a lot of glucose from a pathway that’s not GLUT4,” said Judith A. Heiny, PhD, the study’s co-corresponding author and professor emerita in the Division of Neurobiology and Integrative Physiology in UC’s Department of Biomedical Sciences, whose laboratory led the research.

The researchers named the newly identified pathway mSGLT. It shares properties with SGLT2, a glucose transporter in the kidneys that is already targeted by widely used diabetes medications such as Jardiance. These drugs lower blood sugar by increasing the amount of glucose expelled through urine. Targeting a similar transport mechanism in muscles could offer another way to remove excess glucose from the bloodstream.

“This insulin-independent process uses a glucose transport protein in skeletal muscle and may offer a drug target for controlling blood sugar,” said Heiny. “The skeletal musculature is the natural depot for glucose. It has a huge capacity to regulate blood sugar, which can be a struggle for those with diabetes and insulin resistance.”

“A therapy that targets glucose uptake by skeletal muscles could be as impactful as SGLT2 inhibitors that lower blood sugar by stimulating the kidneys to excrete excess glucose in the urine,” said Natalie Norman, PhD, the study’s first author. Norman contributed to the research as a UC graduate student and is now a postdoctoral researcher at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden.

Working with collaborators at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, the team also developed a new technique for measuring glucose uptake using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), an analytical technique that could have applications beyond diabetes research.

“I expect our method will be ideal for studying biological processes that require simultaneous tracking of multiple molecules,” said Julio Landero, PhD, the study’s co-corresponding author and associate professor and director of a trace metals lab at Mount Sinai.

Although the researchers have established how the pathway behaves in isolated animal muscles, they have yet to identify the specific transport protein responsible or determine whether targeting it can improve blood sugar regulation.

“This study defines the core properties of mSGLT in muscle. Studies are underway to identify the gene and protein at the molecular level,” said Heiny.

Reference: “Insulin-independent glucose uptake into mouse skeletal muscle by a sodium/glucose linked transporter” by Natalie J. Norman, Tatiana L. Radzyukevich, Peter W. Chomczynski, Michal Rymaszewski, Izabela D. Fokt, Waldemar Priebe, Lucas Schmidt, Tiffany Zhu, Bryan Mackenzie, Julio A. Landero and Judith A. Heiny, 19 November 2026, Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-10848-y

The National Institutes of Health, the UC College of Medicine and private philanthropy funded this research.

#6297. Cancer Cells Are Turning Antioxidants Into Weapons Against the Immune System

A newly discovered weakness in cancer cells could open the door to treatments that help the immune system overcome tumors that have resisted immunotherapy.

Cancer immunotherapy has helped some patients fight even advanced cancers, yet many tumors still find ways to escape the immune system. Researchers have now uncovered one possible reason why. Cancer cells can release a protein that removes chemical signals needed by the very immune cells trying to destroy them.

The finding, published in the journal Science, points to a potential new target for cancer treatment. It also challenges a familiar assumption about antioxidants, which are generally associated with protecting cells from damage.

At the center of the discovery are reactive oxygen species (ROS), often called free radicals. These molecules have long been linked to aging, DNA damage, and cancer. In small amounts, however, they serve another purpose. Cancer-fighting immune cells called T cells rely on ROS to activate and attack tumors.

Researchers found that some cancers exploit this dependency by releasing an antioxidant enzyme called peroxiredoxin-1 (PRDX1). The protein removes ROS from the surrounding environment, depriving T cells of signals they need to function.

“One of the surprising findings is that antioxidants aren’t always beneficial in the context of cancer,” said Robert L. Eil, M.D., a physician-scientist who co-led the research. “While reactive oxygen species sound threatening, T cells actually need them to perform their tumor-fighting job. What we found is that tumors can exploit the T cell’s dependency by removing the reactive oxygen species the immune system depends on.”

Eil is an associate professor of surgery in the Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU) School of Medicine and a member of the OHSU Knight Cancer Institute. The study was conducted alongside investigators at the University of Cambridge.

The researchers uncovered the mechanism by examining tumor interstitial fluid, the liquid surrounding cells within tumors. They found high levels of PRDX1, creating an antioxidant-rich environment that could interfere with the immune response.

To determine whether the protein was directly helping cancer survive, the team used CRISPR gene-editing technology to prevent cancer cells from producing PRDX1. Without the enzyme, immune activity increased and tumor growth declined across multiple experimental models.

In one melanoma model, the immune system rejected tumors lacking PRDX1 without additional treatment. In other models, removing the protein made previously resistant tumors respond to immune checkpoint blockade, a type of immunotherapy that helps T cells recognize and attack cancer.

The researchers also looked for evidence of the same process in humans. They analyzed published data from human cancer cell lines, studied gene activity across thousands of tumors, and measured PRDX1 in fluid collected from patient tumors. All three approaches provided evidence that human cancers release PRDX1 into their surroundings, where it can suppress T cell activity.

“We tend to think of reactive oxygen species purely as damaging byproducts of metabolism. But we are increasingly understanding that ROS have important functions within cells, and T cells require them to activate,” said Alexander J. Wesolowski, Ph.D., the study’s first author and a researcher in the Department of Pathology at the University of Cambridge. “Our study develops this picture, revealing that tumors can exploit this very dependency to evade elimination.”

The team also found that cancer cells increased PRDX1 production during a process called immunoediting. As tumors evolve under pressure from the immune system, they can develop characteristics that help them survive. Producing more of this antioxidant protein appears to be one way they may strengthen their defenses.

The researchers describe the mechanism as a previously unrecognized “redox checkpoint,” referring to the way tumors manipulate ROS levels to suppress immune activity.

Understanding this process could be particularly useful for improving immunotherapy, which remains ineffective for many patients despite its success against certain cancers.

“The immune system has already shown us that it can eradicate advanced cancers in some patients,” Eil said. “The challenge is that current immunotherapies don’t work for most people, and even when they do, complete responses remain relatively uncommon. The more we understand how tumors suppress T cells, the more opportunities we have to design therapies that reverse that suppression.”

Possible treatments could include drugs that neutralize antioxidants released by tumors, therapies that block PRDX1 activity, or engineered immune cells capable of functioning in antioxidant-rich environments. These approaches remain possibilities for future research rather than established treatments.

“What’s exciting is that we’ve identified a target nobody was really looking for before,” Eil said. “This doesn’t put a drug in patients’ hands tomorrow, but it gives us an entirely new pathway to pursue. Discovering new targets is how future treatments begin.”

Eil and his collaborators plan to continue investigating how tumors weaken immune responses and whether those defenses can be overcome with next-generation immunotherapies, including engineered T cell treatments.

“This is one more victory against ignorance in understanding why cancers are so difficult to treat,” Eil said. “Every time we uncover a new way tumors suppress the immune system, we gain another opportunity to fight back. That’s how better treatments are built.”

Reference: “Tumor-derived antioxidants suppress immunity by depriving T cells of reactive oxygen species” by Alexander J. Wesolowski, Ardon M. Pillay, Panagiota Vardaka, Rabab Nasrallah, Randy Greaves, Housaiyin Li, Iliana Loffreda, Chelsea Jenkin, Andrew M. James, Alica Nübling, Christopher J. Ward, Teresa von Linde, Alberto G. Conti, Sheue-Fen Tzeng, Layla Dahmani, Alexander C. Evans, Sarah K. Whiteside, Yumi Yamashita-Kanemaru, Charlotte J. Imianowski, Jie Yang, Ignacio Moraga Gonzalez, Jack Chapman, Aws Al-Deka, Klaus Okkenhaug, Michael P. Murphy, Bartlomiej Swiatczak, Geoffrey Guittard, Enrico Lugli, Lukas Flatz, Ping-Chih Ho, Robert L. Eil and Rahul Roychoudhuri, 3 September 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.adz8203

Start by considering what you want to power during an emergency, like a refrigerator, a computer setup, or the entire house. Or, if you're camping or on a job site, consider the devices you want to power or recharge, such as power tools or camping gear like portable refrigerators.

Then consider the type of generator or power station you want. Fuel-based generators can run as long as you have enough fuel, but they’re loud and must be run outside because they emit potentially dangerous fumes. #6295. New Discovery Could Transform How We Treat Chronic Back Pain

Restoring a protein that declines in aging spinal discs reduced DNA damage in human cells in the lab, revealing a potential new target for back pain treatments.

For people living with persistent back pain, everyday activities such as walking, bending, or even sitting comfortably can become difficult. New research from the University of Utah points toward a possible way to address one of the underlying causes of age-related back pain by protecting the cells that keep spinal discs healthy.

Spinal discs are cushion-like structures between vertebrae that allow the spine to move. In a study published in Aging Cell, researchers found that older and damaged discs contained lower levels of a protein called BLST, which is encoded by the ZNF865 gene. The study is the first to characterize the function of both the gene and its protein.

To understand whether declining BLST levels contribute to disc deterioration, the researchers used CRISPR, a gene-editing tool that can be used to regulate the activity of specific genes. Restoring BLST production in human disc cells reduced signs of cellular aging and DNA damage, while decreasing its activity in mouse and rat models led to disc degeneration and pain-related behaviors. The findings suggest that BLST helps maintain healthy spinal discs by protecting cells from damage and dysfunction as they age.

“This paper directly shows a novel understanding that DNA damage is a driver of back pain, and that we can regulate BLST therapeutically with CRISPR,” said Robby D. Bowles, the study’s lead researcher and an associate professor of biomedical engineering. “Back pain is the number three leading cause of disability as measured by disability-adjusted life years, only behind cardiac disease and drug use disorders.”

Although increasing BLST activity could eventually offer a way to prevent or treat age-related back pain, additional preclinical studies and, ultimately, clinical trials are needed to determine whether targeting the protein with CRISPR is safe and effective in people.

The research brought together Bowles and members of his laboratory in the John and Marcia Price College of Engineering, specialists in orthopedics and arthritis at the Spencer Fox Eccles School of Medicine, and researchers at Huntsman Cancer Institute at the University of Utah.

Because DNA damage is involved in numerous diseases, the discovery could have applications well beyond spinal health.

“It has been the highlight of my career to work on a protein that was unknown and be the first to identify its function,” Bowles said. “While this work focuses on its application to back pain, the mechanisms identified have the potential to be applied to treat cancer, neurodegeneration, and any disease in which DNA damage is involved.”

Further research is needed to establish whether the protective mechanisms observed in spinal disc cells also play a role in age-related cancers.

“The fact that a single gene can restore normal cell function and reverse aging-related effects is incredible,” said Jason Gertz, a professor in the Department of Oncological Sciences at the University of Utah and co-leader of the Genomics, Epigenetics, and Metabolism Program at Huntsman Cancer Institute. “BLST is widely expressed across tissues and could be a promising target for cancer treatment and prevention, since boosting BLST activity should improve the repair of DNA damage and the overall health of aging cells.”

Reference: “ZNF865 (BLST) a Novel Regulator of DNA Damage and Cell Senescence in Back Pain” by Christian Lewis, Hunter Levis, Jonah Holbrook, Jacob T. Polaski, Timothy D. Jacobsen, Josh Mizels, Molly Czachor, Sarah E. Gullbrand, Brian Diekman, James C. Iatridis, Jason Gertz, Brandon Lawrence and Robby D. Bowles, 9 October 2026, Aging Cell. DOI: 10.1111/acel.70754

November's full Beaver Moon rises on Tuesday, Nov. 24, giving us a preview of the spectacular Christmas Eve supermoon coming next month.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Tuesday (Nov. 24) to indicate that the full Beaver Moon rises tonight.

November’s full moon, known as the "Beaver Moon," will rise in the east at dusk tonight (Nov. 24), marking the first of three consecutive supermoons.

It will be the third and final full moon of fall in the Northern Hemisphere and the first in a series of unusually close full moons that includes December's spectacular Christmas supermoon — the closest full moon since 2018. These bright moons are just some of the many winter skywatching highlights headed our way in the coming months.

The Beaver Moon gets its name from the time of year when nocturnal beavers in North America traditionally build dams and prepare for winter under the full moon, according to TimeandDate. Other nicknames include the Frost Moon and Snow Moon, and the Anishinaabeg people in North America call it Baashkaakodin Giizis — the Freezing Moon — according to the Center for Native American Studies.

The moon will reach its full phase at 9:53 a.m. ET on Tuesday, when it will be below the horizon in North America. The best time to see the Beaver Moon is at moonrise that evening, as it rises in the east around the same time the sun sets in the west. That's when the moon will appear against a relatively bright twilight sky, making it easier to appreciate its size and color.

The moon will appear full on Monday and Wednesday as well, but Tuesday offers the best opportunity to see it rise during twilight.

The Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, according to EarthSky. A supermoon occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon being relatively close to Earth in its elliptical orbit. The moon's distance from Earth changes throughout the month. On average, the moon is 238,900 miles (384,472 kilometers) from Earth. When a full moon occurs near perigee, or its closest point during its orbit, it appears slightly larger and brighter than usual. #6292. Security Footage Catches Two Zoo Gorillas Forming a “Living Ladder” To Outsmart an Electric Fence

Two zoo gorillas repeatedly teamed up for food despite rarely spending time together, showing that a shared effort does not always end with a shared meal.

A leafy branch was out of reach for two gorillas at the Ramat Gan Safari, and an electric barrier around the trunk blocked a direct climb. The female western lowland gorillas, half-sisters Amelia and Lisha, formed a “living ladder,” with Lisha providing a steady back for Amelia to stand on.

The most extensively documented event came to light in September 2024, when keepers noticed the pair peacefully eating bark and leaves from a large branch that had previously been beyond their reach. Staff reviewed security camera footage to find out how they had obtained it.

The recording showed Amelia walking over and climbing onto a rock beneath a Peltophorum dubium tree. Lisha joined her and stood firmly on all fours on the rock. Amelia then climbed onto Lisha’s back, stood upright, and reached up to grasp and break off a branch approximately 4.5 meters, or 15 feet, above the ground. The rock, Lisha’s stable posture, and Amelia’s reach together made the branch accessible.

Researchers documented three events involving the same pair in 2021, 2024, and 2025, with each gorilla performing the same role every time. Neither had been trained to perform the maneuver. The team describes their behavior as a rare example of spontaneous cooperation between adult gorillas, with a clear division of roles.

Published in Primates, the study was led by Michael Levitzky and Prof. Israel Hershkovitz of the Department of Anatomy and Anthropology at the Gray Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences and the Dan David Center for Human Evolution and Biohistory Research at Tel Aviv University.

Yehonatan Samocha, Head of the Primate Section at the Ramat Gan Safari (Zoological Center Tel Aviv-Ramat Gan), said, “At the Ramat Gan Safari we have observed and studied animal behaviors for years, closely following their relationships, social bonds, and fascinating capabilities. Particularly among great apes, including gorillas, we repeatedly encounter behaviors that demonstrate high intelligence, learning ability, problem-solving, complex communication, and cooperation.

“This is why we are so thrilled, though not necessarily surprised, by the cooperation between Amelia and Lisha. We are familiar with their abilities and understand how intelligent and curious they are, and how capable they are of learning from one another and working together. Sometimes, our surprise tells us more about our expectations of animals than their actual abilities. The study’s great importance lies in providing scientific documentation and analysis for observations and behaviors we encounter in our daily work, allowing us to enhance our knowledge of gorillas, their social world, and their cognitive abilities.”

In the June 2025 footage, Lisha positioned herself with her back toward Amelia, who was not observed using force. Levitzky, who initiated and led the study, explained how the recording helped the researchers interpret Lisha’s participation.

“When I first watched the footage, it was clear to me that this was something extraordinary. What I find fascinating is that Leisha did more than simply serve as a ‘step’ for Amelia. She appeared to participate actively and willingly in solving the problem, approaching on her own initiative and positioning herself in exactly the right place, without Amelia physically guiding her. This is the difference between using another individual as a tool and true cooperation, in which both individuals work together toward the same goal.

“For years, gorillas were considered less cognitively sophisticated than other great apes. As more observations like these accumulate, we will be able to deepen and refine our understanding of their social and cognitive abilities. Future studies involving systematic documentation and audio recordings could help us decipher how they coordinate with one another, and perhaps also teach us something about the roots of cooperation in our own species.”

The sisters generally spend little time together, sleep in separate night quarters, and rarely groom one another. Their teamwork also had different outcomes at feeding time. Although keepers reported peaceful sharing after the 2024 event, Amelia alone ate the vegetation in the observed 2025 sequence, showing that cooperating to obtain food did not necessarily lead to sharing it.

Hershkovitz said, “Our observations reveal how two gorillas can join forces and assume complementary roles to solve a problem that neither can solve on her own. It is particularly intriguing that this cooperation recurs even though the two do not usually display much closeness, and even when the food is not shared between them afterward. These observations are important for understanding human evolution because they offer an explanation, albeit a partial one, for how we survived on the savanna – through social support and a high level of cooperation that can occur even without language or preplanning. Although the number of observations is small, they offer a window into gorillas’ ability to learn from experience, coordinate their actions, and draw on one another and their surroundings to achieve a shared goal.”

The study involved only two gorillas and three documented events. The available footage could not establish whether they communicated through vocalizations or subtle gestures, or whether they planned their actions in advance.

Reference: “Cooperation in adult female western lowland gorillas: complex problem-solving through learned spatial affordances and mutual agency” by Michael Levitzky, and Israel Hershkovitz, 24 October 2026, Primates. DOI: 10.1007/s10329-026-01297-6

#6291. Solo meerkats can find their way back home

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Meerkats live, forage and raise their young in large groups. But they’ve still got solo skills

To test meerkats’ solo navigating skills, researchers outfitted the animals with GPS trackers, separated them from their packs, and followed their journeys back home.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, says Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin says. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she says. But that’s not what the team discovered.

In separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin says.)

Neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin says. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she says, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

M. Martin et al. Ubiquitously efficient solo navigation in group-living meerkats. Journal of Experimental Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1242/jeb.252200

#6289. America’s Data Centers Have a Hidden Death Toll, MIT Researchers Warn

An MIT analysis estimates that powering America’s data centers contributed to hundreds of premature deaths in a single year, with rural populations facing greater risks than city dwellers.

As artificial intelligence drives the rapid construction of data centers across the United States, concerns about their environmental impact are taking on a new dimension. The electricity needed to keep these facilities running around the clock can increase air pollution in communities far from where the data centers themselves are built, potentially putting the health of people who live nowhere near them at risk.

Researchers at MIT estimate that air pollution associated with data center electricity consumption contributed to approximately 650 premature deaths in the United States in 2023 alone. Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas had the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita, even though much of the electricity demand was concentrated in northern Virginia and Texas. Rates in Virginia and Texas were only about half those in most Midwestern states.

“When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors. But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region. Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” says Noelle Selin, senior author of the study, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS), and director of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that data centers’ electricity needs accounted for about 4 percent of total U.S. energy demand in 2023 and approximately 4.4 percent of the nation’s overall emissions. Those proportions have likely grown as more facilities have been built.

Determining who bears the health consequences of that growing demand is complicated by the interconnected nature of the nation’s power grid. A data center in Virginia, for example, may increase electricity production at power plants in the Ohio Valley, where a greater proportion of older coal and natural gas plants produce higher levels of emissions.

“Different regions have different mixes of power. If you turn on a major new demand source, by plugging a data center into the grid, you might have to fire up your really dirty power plant to meet that new demand,” Selin says.

The pollution can then travel into neighboring states, where local atmospheric conditions can make matters worse. In agricultural regions such as Iowa and Nebraska, ammonia released from fertilizer promotes the formation of fine particulate matter (PM2.5), microscopic airborne particles that can cause heart attacks, strokes, and lung disease.

The estimated health consequences also extend to Kansas, South Dakota, Missouri, and Arkansas. Overall, the researchers found that rural populations face a significantly higher estimated mortality risk from data center electricity demand than urban populations.

To understand how these risks are distributed, the team developed a model that tracks electricity production and transmission between regions on an hourly basis. While many previous studies relied on average power grid emissions, the researchers assumed that data centers operated around the clock and identified which individual generators would respond to their additional electricity needs.

“Generators that respond to additional electricity demand are often natural gas plants, although the response varies by place and hour,” says Yuang (Albert) Chen, an MIT graduate student and co-author of the study.

“It was a challenge to gather all the data,” Chen says. “There are more than 10,000 generators in the U.S. grid, and we needed to make sure the data provided for each generator is valid and validated across other data sources.”

The researchers calculated emissions of nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide from individual generators. Both pollutants contribute to the formation of fine particulate matter, while nitrogen oxides also help produce ground-level ozone, commonly associated with smog.

Using a separate atmospheric model, the team simulated how these pollutants formed and traveled across regions. They then drew on epidemiological research linking air pollution to premature death to estimate the resulting health impacts.

Of the approximately 650 premature deaths estimated for 2023, 513 were attributed to fine particulate matter and 137 to smog. Together, they represented about 5.3 percent of all estimated electricity-related premature deaths nationwide.

“While it is not surprising that any additional source of air pollution will result in mortalities, with data centers, when and where these deaths are occurring are different than you might expect,” Selin says.

As companies continue to expand their computing infrastructure, the findings suggest that decisions about where to build data centers and how to power them need to account for public health well beyond the immediate surroundings.

“When people are thinking about data center siting and operations, it is important to consider more than just things like land and energy prices. They should also take air quality considerations into the equation,” Chen says. “This is a good baseline to think about where we should build data centers and how we should supply those data centers with electricity.”

The researchers hope to investigate the air quality consequences of a growing industry trend in which data centers incorporate their own on-site power plants. They could also examine whether adjusting when these facilities consume electricity could reduce their impact on air quality.

Reference: “Spatially distributed air quality and health impacts of data center electricity demand in the United States” by Yuang Chen, Shen Wang, Juan Ramon L Senga, Andrew Scott White, Anthony YH Wong, Lyssa M Freese, Michelle L Bell and Noelle E Selin, 19 November 2026, Environmental Research Letters. DOI: 10.1088/1748-9326/aebbd4

This research was funded, in part, by the MIT Energy Initiative Society of Energy Scholars and the MIT Martin Family Society of Fellows for Sustainability.

Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity.

This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern, a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery.

Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79.

"It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sune Nielsen, a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study. "Very far from it."

A fish in the genus Pseudoliparis in an image taken during during a dive by the Jason/Medea ROV at 20,659 feet (6,297 m).

The Challenger Deep is in the remote western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench. There, the Pacific oceanic plate pushes under the Mariana oceanic plate in a process called subduction. At the trench where the two plates meet, the ocean floor plunges down 6.8 miles (10.9 kilometers). Mount Everest could fit in the chasm, with room to spare.

Geoscientists aren't sure why the trench is so dizzyingly deep, but they have turned up some clues. For instance, there is a tear in the Pacific Plate that allows one narrow strip of the plate to subduct particularly rapidly. The curvature of the plate is also very steep, perhaps because the rocks of the Mariana and Pacific plates aren't very strongly connected to each other, allowing the Pacific Plate to dive steeply and flex freely.

The new findings, reported Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, suggest that volcanism and magma also may play a role, Stern said. The researchers were exploring a segment of the Challenger Deep's forearc, a roughly 120-mile-wide (200 km) expanse that sits between the trench itself and the volcanic arc created by the subduction zone. These volcanic arcs are standard subduction zone features; for example, Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier are part of the volcanic arc of the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But though there are some volcanoes north of Challenger Deep along the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep segment of the trench is odd in that there is not an organized volcanic arc there. Instead, there's an ocean ridge. Regardless, the space between this ridge and the trench was expected to be volcanically quiet because there is not usually enough heat in that region of a subduction zone to melt magma.

Nevertheless, the cameras on the deep-diving remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which went to the site in 2014, caught strange, pancake-like rock features at three different spots in a 60-mile (100 km) stretch of the trench. Samples brought on board the ship revealed rock embedded with volcanic glass and a pyroclastic flow texture.

A sea cucumber in an image from the Jason/Medea dive at 12,726 feet (3879 m).

The researchers are currently getting the rock dated, but volcanic glass usually erodes quickly in the ocean, Stern said, so the presence of glass suggests the eruptions were fairly recent. "They're not yesterday," he said, "but I don't think they're a million years old."

The pressure of the water at the depths of the flows is equivalent to 592 atmospheres of Earth stacked on top of one another. Typically, that kind of pressure keeps a lid on the dissolved water and carbon dioxide in magma that expands rapidly to cause explosive eruptions. Thus, Stern said, the eruptions by the Challenger Deep may have been driven by a supercritical fluid ‪—‬ a weird state sort of in between a gas and a liquid.

"We just don’t know how those magmas will behave at those water depths," said Stephen Self, a volcanologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the study.

The mission's observations also suggest that the crust of this region is extending, or stretching, in two different ways. To the east, the stretch is caused by a mechanical pulling apart of the crust. To the west, volcanic eruptions are stretching the crust. It's a perplexing finding, Nielsen said, without a clear explanation.

Stern and his colleagues suspect that the two plates are starting a new subduction zone in this western part. That would be an exciting finding; subduction zones move around over tens of millions of years, and researchers don't know much about how new ones start. The geochemical studies of the rocks that Stern and his team pulled up could answer questions about where the lava that made the pyroclastic flows came from and why this bizarre region can generate magma where none should be.

"This region is really, really unusual for our planet, and there is quite a bit of, 'What, really? Wait, how is that? OK, yeah, I guess maybe.'" Nielsen said. "So obviously, I find it super interesting."

Stern, R. J., Pujana, I., Anderson, M. K., Chin, E., Dygert, N., Harigane, Y., Le Roux, V., Leybourne, M., Ohara, Y., Okumura, T., Segee-Wright, G., & Etheridge, E. (n.d.). ROVing in the deep: Tectonic and magmatic complexities of the challenger deep forearc segment, southern mariana convergent margin. Frontiers in Earth Science, 14, 1929806. https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2026.1929806

#6286. Earth’s Lakes Are Changing in Unison – and Scientists Are Worried

Lakes play an important role in regulating Earth’s carbon cycle, and scientists warn that environmental changes occurring across many lakes at once could amplify global climate risks.

Lakes around the world are increasingly changing in step, a trend that could weaken a natural buffer against environmental disruption. A new study found that this synchronization has accelerated markedly since 2000.

The characteristics of a lake’s watershed, the land that drains into it, have historically helped buffer its ecosystem against broader environmental changes. Lakes fluctuated independently, a pattern known as “spatial asynchrony” that spread ecological disturbances across time and space.

A team led by Prof. Ke Zhang of the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (NIGLAS) combined century-scale sediment records with continuous satellite observations from approximately 2,000 lakes. Alongside growing synchrony, the researchers found a significant decline in network modularity, meaning the lake network was becoming less divided into groups with distinct patterns of change.

The researchers used water clarity and phytoplankton biomass, the mass of microscopic organisms that use sunlight to make food, as proxies for lake metabolic activity. These indicators provide an indirect view of how lake ecosystems process energy and nutrients. Their growing synchrony suggests that the underlying carbon, nutrient, and biodiversity dynamics they reflect may also be becoming more synchronized.

The study attributes this shift to environmental telecoupling, connections through which climate extremes such as heatwaves and socioeconomic pressures link changes across distant regions. The authors describe this increasingly linked response to large-scale environmental change as a new hallmark of the Anthropocene, a term used to describe a world profoundly shaped by human activity.

Although lakes cover less than 2% of Earth’s surface, they help regulate global carbon and nutrient cycles and biodiversity. Losing the differences in how they respond to environmental pressures could therefore have consequences well beyond individual watersheds.

“This loss of buffering capacity transforms lakes from passive, regionally distinct systems into active amplifiers of global environmental risks. Synchronized lakes can concentrate biophysical fluxes, potentially triggering high-amplitude global pulses, such as simultaneous greenhouse gas emissions or widespread aquatic hypoxia, thereby exacerbating the triple planetary crisis,” Zhang said.

Aquatic hypoxia means a shortage of oxygen in the water. The “triple planetary crisis” refers to climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution.

Water management has traditionally treated lakes as isolated local resources, creating what the researchers describe as a “scale mismatch” between governance and the processes shaping these ecosystems. Zhang and his co-authors propose treating interconnected lake networks as a dynamically coupled “Planetary Commons.” Their objective is to protect the local ecological processes that maintain variation across landscapes, without seeking to eliminate synchrony.

To put that idea into practice, the team introduced a framework called Strategic Planetary Lake Areas (SPLAs). By tracking large-scale measures of synchrony and modularity, policymakers could identify priority regions, including regional groups of lakes whose behavior is rapidly converging. These areas could become candidates for targeted polycentric governance, an approach involving multiple centers of decision-making.

“This research not only redefines the critical importance of inland waters in global change studies but also introduces a macroscale dimension to international sustainable development agendas,” Zhang said. “The work emphasizes that preserving the diversity of ecological responses is essential for maintaining long-term Earth-system stability in an increasingly interconnected world.”

Reference: “Global lake synchrony signals rising planetary-scale ecological coupling” by Ke Zhang, Yaoyao Han, Lindsey Gillson, Xiaoling Zhang, Suzanne McGowan, Michael E. Meadows, Yuan Jin, Luki Subehi, John A. Dearing, David P. Hamilton, Yan Zhao, Lian Pin Koh and David Taylor, 16 November 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2611874123

“The authors describe this increasingly linked response to large-scale environmental change as a new hallmark of the Anthropocene.”

The article doesn’t really support their claim of “increasing synchrony.” This sounds more like assigning a scapegoat than explaining what is driving the alleged changes. It appears to me that the relationship is best described by a U-shaped function rather than a linear, long-term trend. The index graph that is most U-like is the one going back farthest in time, suggesting some periodicity related to time.

The R^2 value in all cases is less than 0.5, and in most cases less than 0.2. That means that the variance in the dependent variable that is explained by the changes in the independent variable is less than the probability of getting a ‘Head’ in a coin flip. That doesn’t convince me that they really understand what is going on. But the buzzword salad had all the right words and conclusions to get published!

#6285. A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Unlike in the Dr. Seuss tale, a swollen heart can be an alarming sign of stress or disease

The Grinch’s change of heart turned him from grumpy to radiating joy. Is such a transformation possible in real life?

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

“They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” says the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really big in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Heart size is generally pegged to body size, says Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”

In one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

Smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson says. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

As the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

There are many ways a heart can grow, says Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

“Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson says. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

Some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand says, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”

Stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson says.

There is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too big to pump blood.

So instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson says. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.)

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

Pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as big as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

Once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

But becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”

#6284. Losing Weight but Getting Less Healthy? Study Reveals a Dark Side of Keto

Mice that lost weight on a very low-protein keto diet also developed fatty liver and lost muscle, highlighting the limitations of weight as a measure of health.

Ketogenic diets have become a popular approach to weight loss, despite conflicting research on their metabolic benefits. A new study in mice suggests that two often overlooked factors may help explain these inconsistencies: the amount of protein in the diet and the genetic makeup of the animals eating it. The findings also raise questions about whether losing weight on a keto diet necessarily means becoming healthier.

The research, published in Cell Metabolism, began when first author Zhaoyue Zhang, a postdoctoral fellow in the Friedman lab, noticed considerable variation in the protein content of ketogenic diets. Although these diets are generally high in fat and extremely low in carbohydrates, their protein content could be contributing to differences in metabolic outcomes.

Zhang and her colleagues systematically tested diets containing different proportions of fat and protein. After four weeks on a ketogenic diet containing just 5% protein, mice belonging to C57Bl/6J, the most commonly used laboratory mouse strain, reduced their food intake by approximately 40% and lost weight. Mice fed an otherwise similar diet containing 10% protein ate more and gained weight. Both groups produced ketones, molecules generated when the body relies heavily on fat for fuel, suggesting that ketosis alone could not account for the difference.

“The result was so striking,” Zhang says.

A closer look at the mice that lost weight revealed a more complicated picture. Although their glucose tolerance, or ability to manage changes in blood sugar, improved, they also developed fatty liver. Much of their weight loss was associated with reductions in lean mass, including muscle.

To understand what was suppressing the animals’ appetite, the researchers investigated GDF15, a hormone released in response to cellular stress that can act on the brain to reduce food intake. When they conducted an experiment using genetically modified mice lacking GDF15, even the control mice unexpectedly failed to lose weight on the low-protein diet.

“At first, I was a bit panicked,” Zhang says. “We had repeated the same experiment many times, and all of a sudden it didn’t work.”

Retracing her steps, Zhang discovered that the genetically modified mice belonged to a different substrain, C57Bl/6N, which shares approximately 99.9% of its genome with the mice used in the earlier experiments.

“This realization was key, and it became the starting point for the rest of the study,” Zhang says.

The researchers eventually identified two genes that helped explain the difference: NNT, which protects cells against oxidative stress, and NLRP12, which helps regulate inflammation. The mice susceptible to weight loss, known as B6J, carried mutations in both genes. Feeding them the low-protein ketogenic diet triggered stress and inflammatory responses in the liver, accompanied by rising levels of GDF15 and an inflammation-associated protein called LCN2. Both proteins can influence appetite through their effects on the brain.

Restoring NNT function in B6J mice caused them to eat more and lose less weight. Conversely, disabling both genes in the genetically similar B6NJ mice, which normally carry functioning versions of both genes, caused them to eat less and lose weight. Treatment with N-acetylcysteine, an antioxidant with anti-inflammatory properties, also lowered circulating levels of GDF15 and LCN2, increased food intake, and reduced weight loss.

Zhang cautions that the findings cannot be directly applied to humans, particularly because the 5% protein diet contained substantially less protein than most ketogenic diets used in clinical trials. Future trials could benefit from paying closer attention to both dietary protein content and genetic differences among participants, while looking beyond weight loss and blood sugar control when assessing metabolic health.

The researchers now want to investigate whether other genetic factors influence responses to ketogenic diets and whether the changes they observed can be reversed once the diet is discontinued.

Reference: “Macronutrient composition and genetic background determine the response to a ketogenic diet in mice” by Zhaoyue Zhang, Alexandre Moura-Assis, Shanshan Liu, Alon Millet, Jordan Shaked, Divya Rajan, Katelin Chen, Anduena Toci, Chloe Schaefer, Ijeoma Obi, Sebastian Carrasco, Sandra Kelly Atkinson, Francois Marchildon, Hanan Alwaseem, Michael Isay-Del Viscio, Henrik Molina, Paul Cohen, Kivanc Birsoy and Jeffrey Friedman, 18 November 2026, Cell Metabolism. DOI: 10.1016/j.cmet.2026.10.017

This silver pepper shaker reveals the Romans' love of the spice and the lengths they would go to procure it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The pepper shaker was discovered as part of an ancient Roman hoard.

Where it is from: Hoxne, Suffolk, England

In 1992, a farmer in the village of Hoxne in southeastern England was searching for a lost hammer with a metal detector when he stumbled upon a massive hoard of more than 15,000 ancient Roman coins, jewelry and tableware. Among the artifacts in the Hoxne hoard was a silver spice container in the shape of an imperial lady.

The artifact, named the Empress, is one of four pepper pots ("piperatoria" in Latin) discovered in the Hoxne hoard, according to the British Museum. The silver container stands about 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is decorated with gold around the woman's eyes, mouth, hair and accessories, including a scroll in her left hand. The woman's elaborate hairstyle helps date the creation of the pepper pot to the fourth century, but experts think the hoard may have been buried in the early fifth century, when Roman rule in Britain was ending.

At the bottom of the pot, which rests on a four-legged base, there is a disc that can be set at three positions: wide open, closed and partly open. The pot would have been filled in the open position with cracked pepper and then used in the partly open position for sprinkling the spice over food.

The ancient Romans were huge fans of pepper, Neil MacGregor, former director of the British Museum, wrote in "A History of the World in 100 Objects" (Penguin Books, 2010). Pepper didn't grow in the Roman Empire, so merchants procured it from India. This made it an expensive spice, and filling up the pepper pot would have been costly.

A wealthy Romano-British family likely used the pepper pot as elaborate tableware, MacGregor wrote. It is unclear whom the Empress was meant to depict, but researchers don't think it features a member of the Roman imperial family. However, the fact that she holds a scroll could indicate that she was both wealthy and well educated.

The ancient family who lived near Hoxne seems to have left its wealth behind during the breakdown of Roman rule in Britain, since the pepper pot was found in a chest that contained dozens of pieces of silverware, 29 pieces of gold jewelry, and more than 15,000 coins.

"This was the mobile wealth of a rich Roman family — precisely the type of person who is in danger when the state fails," MacGregor wrote.

#6282. Scientists Uncover a Potential Root Cause of the Global Allergy Epidemic

Scientists have identified a potential biological mechanism that could explain how seemingly unrelated environmental factors contribute to the growing prevalence of allergies.

Allergies may begin with an energy crisis inside the cells that protect the body from the outside world, rather than a malfunction of the immune system. An extensive analysis led by Griffith University researchers challenges decades of conventional thinking about allergic diseases and proposes a potential biological origin for conditions ranging from eczema to food allergies.

The researchers identified abnormalities involving mitochondria, the structures responsible for producing much of the energy cells need to function. Their findings suggest that epithelial cells, which form protective barriers along the skin, gut, nose, lungs, and esophagus, may struggle to meet environmental and metabolic demands, triggering an excessive immune response.

“For 60 years, we’ve taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around,” said study lead Professor Peter Smith, a clinical immunologist from Griffith’s School of Medicine and Dentistry.

The team examined what it describes as the largest collection of multi-omic allergy data known to the researchers, drawing on 116 case-control cohorts and data from 3,776 patients. Multi-omic analysis combines different types of molecular information to identify biological patterns that might otherwise go undetected.

Scientists may have discovered the hidden cause of allergies. Credit: Professor Peter Smith, Griffith University

“Allergy diseases, which now affect up to one in three children, may start one step earlier as a power failure in the mitochondria of the epithelial cells which form the body’s barrier surfaces,” Professor Smith said.

“The barrier cell can’t meet the energy and stress demands of the modern environment so raises the alarm too easily, and the immune events we recognize as an allergy, follow.

“It could help to explain why some children have eczema, food allergies, hay fever, asthma and related conditions.”

The strongest evidence emerged in eosinophilic esophagitis, an allergic inflammatory disease affecting the esophagus. Across all 13 independent patient cohorts, researchers found reduced activity in the cellular process responsible for removing damaged mitochondria.

In patients with eczema, abnormalities affecting the skin’s protective barrier and antioxidant defenses appeared even in areas without inflammation. This finding is consistent with the possibility that cellular dysfunction precedes visible symptoms.

However, the mitochondrial signature was not universal. Researchers found only partial evidence of it in hay fever, while the pattern was absent in established asthma and nasal polyps.

The researchers propose that several environmental factors associated with allergies could converge on the same biological vulnerability: the ability of epithelial cells to generate sufficient energy and withstand stress.

Potential contributors include highly processed diets, air pollution, microplastics, detergents, declining dietary fiber intake, and antibiotic exposure early in life.

Associate Professor Nic West, a molecular immunologist from Griffith’s School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences and co-author of the study, said the wide range of factors associated with allergies has made it difficult to develop a unified explanation for their rapid increase within a single generation.

The proposed mechanism could also explain why allergic diseases frequently recur after treatment. Inflammation itself can damage epithelial cells, potentially creating a self-perpetuating cycle of barrier dysfunction and immune activation.

“The research also explains why allergies can relapse,” Associate Professor West said.

“Once inflammation is established it damages the barrier further.

“Today’s drugs act downstream, so the disease often returns when treatment stops as they do not reach the root cause.”

The researchers emphasize that their findings support a hypothesis rather than establish a definitive cause of allergies. Direct measurements of epithelial cell function before symptoms appear will be needed to determine whether mitochondrial dysfunction initiates allergic disease.

“We have spent our careers managing the smoke and for the first time we think we can see the fire, and it is not where everyone was looking,” Professor Smith said.

“This is not a cure but is something we have never had before – a logical starting point.

“The next step is to measure these cells directly in infants before the allergy develops.”

Reference: “The Origins of Allergy: An Outside-In, Bioenergetic Hypothesis” by Peter K. Smith, Nicholas P. West, Stanley Du Preez, Hugh A. Sampson, Peter W. Hellings, David Price, Liam O’Mahony, Carina Venter, Cezmi A. Akdis and Gil Yosipovitch, 29 October 2026, Allergy. DOI: 10.1111/all.70532

#6281. The Book Lover’s Gift Guide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Science News staff loved books about dinosaurs, parenting and numbers in 2026

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science News staff devoured books of all kinds this year, on topics ranging from ecology and evolution to the human brain and mathematics. We covered it all — even a cookbook! These 10 titles rose to the top of our 2026 reading list and could make great gifts for the book lovers in your life. —  Anna Mattson, Assistant Editor

Big thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers. “When I think of big numbers, I usually think of a 1 with a lot of zeroes tacked on the end. But the reality is much more complex than I ever imagined,” says senior physics writer Emily Conover. The book, among Conover’s favorites of the year, “provided me with a new appreciation of our number system and the creative ways mathematicians have expanded it to express ever-larger numbers,” she says. “Plus, contemplating unfathomably large figures makes my own concerns seem insignificant.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with new parents. “Between sleepless nights and poopy diapers, there’s not much to laugh about in the early days of parenting. But I found plenty of humor (and plenty to be grossed out about) in The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” Garcia de Jesús says. “It’s the perfect book to make anyone, parent or otherwise, feel better that we’re not the only animals struggling with our offspring.”

Merritt R. TuretskyW.W. Norton & Company | $29.99

Adventure seekers will lose themselves in the mesmerizing ecosystems at the heart of Bogland, biomedical sciences writer Aimee Cunningham’s favorite book of the year. Ecologist Merritt R. Turetsky immerses readers in these waterlogged landscapes that are often overlooked and underestimated. “I am firmly on team boglands after reading about the beauty and wonder of these ecosystems,” Cunningham says.

Senior writer Meghan Rosen’s favorite book of 2026 is perfect for anyone interested in — or wary of — health and wellness culture. Morbid exposes the lack of science behind a lot of antiaging advice, such as eating like centenarians do and taking “anti­aging” supplements. “Turns out, a lot of it is just plain bunk,” Rosen says. “Skeptical readers will enjoy Newman’s takedowns, which go down smoothly with a healthy dose of humor.”

Senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders’ pick for 2026 is a must-read for any expecting mother, new mother or person looking to learn about how pregnancy and motherhood impact the body. “A Mother’s Brain reads like a scientific love letter to moms, who all too often get overlooked,” she says. Author and neuroscientist Susana Carmona “covers the nascent field of matrescence in lively, vivid chapters. And along the way, she convincingly argues that the maternal brain is compelling, wondrous and still mysterious,” Sanders says.

Those who listen to true crime podcasts or wish spooky season lasted all year long will enjoy Exhumed, an exploration of the lore and medical practices leading up to the 19th century New England vampire panic. “Thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down,” assistant editor Anna Mattson wrote in her online review. Mattson notes that Exhumed, her favorite read of 2026, is littered with bizarre facts that would be perfect for invigorating dull conversations.

For the anthropologist in your life, try The Story of Stories — a deep dive into how technological upheavals have shaped storytelling throughout history. The author provides what Sanders describes as scattershot history lessons in her online review: “Ashton has a knack for pulling out memorable bits from historical records, scientific studies and other sources for readers.”

Alexis Nikole NelsonSimon & Schuster | $35.00

Conover couldn’t pick just one favorite. For people who enjoy getting creative in the kitchen, she recommends Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! “This cookbook provides such a joyful how-to on foraging and eating wild plants,” Conover says. “It helped me see my plant neighbors in a whole new light. And I got to make some tasty treats to share with my family as well.”

Tyrant Lizard Queen is the only work of fiction on our list. But it’s rooted in real science, and stars a Tyrannosaurus rex. Author Riley Black “offers an empathetic look at a real-life creature that experienced hunger and pain, much like the animals that surround us today,” says Science News Explores assistant editor Aaron Tremper, who chose the book as his favorite of 2026. “Black’s penchant for story makes for a thrilling read that fans of Jurassic Park and King Kong can get behind.”

And for those interested in bioethics, we suggest picking up Every Living Creature. Author and physician Joshua D. Mezrich offers a comprehensive look at the field of xenotransplantation, through the stories of courageous doctors and patients who helped make it possible. “At times, the story can feel like a whirlwind, whisking readers across decades and from lab to lab and surgery to surgery,” Rosen wrote in her online review. “But at its core, Every Living Creature is a book about hope.”

#6280. Intermittent Fasting May Not Work the Way Scientists Thought for Liver Health

A clinical trial suggests that improving liver health may require less attention to strict fasting schedules and more emphasis on developing eating habits that people can sustain.

For people using intermittent fasting to reduce fat in the liver, finding a meal schedule that helps them lose weight may be more important than eating at specific times of the day. A new clinical trial found that people who lost at least 5% of their body weight experienced the greatest reductions in liver fat, with no clear advantage to eating earlier or later in the day.

Led by the University of Granada (UGR) and the Public University of Navarra, the multicenter study was published in JHEP Reports and involved 197 adults aged 30 to 60 with overweight or obesity. The research forms part of the doctoral dissertation of Antonio Clavero Jimeno, a predoctoral researcher at the University Joint Institute for Sport and Health (iMUDS) at UGR.

The researchers conducted a secondary analysis of a clinical trial previously published in Nature Medicine. That trial found that participants who practiced intermittent fasting lost an average of 3 to 4 kilograms (6.6 to 8.8 pounds) more than those who received only nutritional recommendations, regardless of their eating schedule. Eating earlier in the day, which in Spain often amounts to skipping dinner, also produced specific improvements in certain measures of blood sugar regulation.

To investigate whether these eating schedules offered additional benefits for liver health, the researchers compared three forms of time-restricted eating (TRE), a type of intermittent fasting that confines food consumption to specific hours of the day.

Participants were randomly assigned to four groups: standard care, early eating (approximately 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.), late eating (2 p.m. to 10 p.m.), and a self-selected eating window (12:20 p.m. to 8 p.m. on average). Over 12 weeks, all four groups received the same nutritional education program based on the Mediterranean diet and healthy lifestyle habits.

The researchers used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure liver fat and examined liver stiffness, liver enzymes, circulating proteins involved in liver metabolism, and other indicators of liver health.

Although liver fat decreased in all three intermittent fasting groups, none experienced statistically significant improvements beyond those achieved through standard care. The timing of meals also made no significant difference to other measures of liver health or the composition and diversity of microorganisms living in the gut.

Approximately 40 to 45% of participants practicing intermittent fasting lost at least 5% of their body weight. Reaching this threshold was associated with significantly greater reductions in liver fat, and most participants who achieved it belonged to the fasting groups. Greater reductions were also observed among people who already had hepatic steatosis, an excessive accumulation of fat in the liver, at the beginning of the study.

“The results do not suggest that intermittent fasting is ineffective, but rather that choosing an early, late, or self-selected fasting window does not appear to provide any additional benefit for liver health,” explain Manuel Dote Montero and Antonio Clavero Jimeno, the study’s first authors.

For the researchers, “the most important factor seems to be choosing a strategy that facilitates clinically significant weight loss and can be sustained over time.”

References: “Time-restricted eating, liver health, and fecal microbiota in adults with overweight or obesity: A randomized controlled trial” by Manuel Dote-Montero, Antonio Clavero-Jimeno, Adrián Cortés-Martín, Amaya Lopez-Pascual, Elisa Merchán-Ramírez, Alba Camacho-Cardenosa, Mara Concepción, Maddi Osés, Alejandro López-Vázquez, Francisco J Amaro-Gahete, Juan J Martin-Olmedo, Lucas Jurado-Fasoli, Alejandro De-la-O, Patricia V García Pérez, Julio Gálvez, Alba Rodriguez-Nogales, Federico Garcia, Carmen Mbongo Habimana, Marcos Jiménez Vázquez, Víctor Manuel Alfaro-Magallanes, Matías A Avila, Jose L Martín-Rodríguez, Rafael Cabeza, Manuel Muñoz-Torres, Idoia Labayen and Jonatan R Ruiz, 7 July 2026, JHEP Reports.
