#6278. Scientists Discover 130-Year-Old Fish Still Swimming in an American River

Some fish swimming in Montana’s Upper Missouri River today may have hatched before the 20th century began. Researchers have confirmed that blue suckers can live up to 130 years, more than three times their previously estimated lifespan of roughly 40 years. The discovery places the species among the longest-lived vertebrates in North America.

The findings, published in Communications Biology, come from a study co-led by Alec Lackmann of the University of Minnesota Duluth, Luke Holmquist of Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks, and Allen Andrews of the University of Hawai’i at Mānoa. By examining microscopic structures inside the fishes’ heads and using a chemical signature left by nuclear weapons testing, the scientists uncovered evidence of extraordinary longevity and a population increasingly dominated by old individuals.

The blue sucker (Cycleptus elongatus) is native to 23 U.S. states but is classified as imperiled in 22 of them. For decades, researchers monitoring the Upper Missouri River have observed increasingly large fish and remarkably few juveniles. The pattern suggests that young blue suckers have struggled to survive and join the adult population.

“For decades, there has been conservation concern for the species across much of its range,” the researchers wrote. “Nonetheless, no validated age-based life history information exists for the species, which is a major knowledge gap.”

To investigate, the team collected and examined nearly 50 blue suckers between 2023 and 2026. More than 60 percent were older than 90 years, and some had survived for approximately 130 years. Their age distribution suggests that successful recruitment of new generations has become less frequent since major dams were installed in the mid-1900s. Habitat fragmentation associated with those dams is a possible contributor, although the study does not establish it as the cause.

The researchers determined the fishes’ ages by examining otoliths, tiny structures commonly called earstones that occur in approximately 97 percent of fish species. These structures grow throughout a fish’s life, accumulating annual layers that scientists can count under a microscope, much like the growth rings of a tree.

Blue suckers presented a technical challenge because their otoliths are exceptionally small. “Blue suckers have extremely small otoliths, smaller than the buffalofishes, but we figured out how to work with them,” Lackmann said.

As the researchers examined the growth layers, they encountered ages that far exceeded established expectations. In fish previously thought to live around four decades, “we were seeing the population had ages up to 130 years old,” Lackmann said. “When age estimates are that much older than previously thought, an additional line of evidence is needed to rigorously test their validity.”

To independently verify the ages, the team turned to bomb radiocarbon dating, a technique that uses the atmospheric changes caused by nuclear weapons testing during the Cold War. Those tests produced a distinctive increase in radioactive carbon-14 that became incorporated into living organisms, including the tissues of fish.

“Thermonuclear bombs that were tested in the mid to late 1950s and early 1960s more than doubled the amount of radiocarbon in the atmosphere,” said Lackmann.

“This left a time-specific marker in organisms that lived through the bomb pulse. And if you’re able to quantify growth bands in an individual (for example, in trees, otoliths of bony fish, etc.) that is estimated to have lived through the bomb pulse, you can actually test to determine if the ages you are quantifying are accurate. Bomb radiocarbon dating is one of the best ways to age-validate long-lived organisms. So that’s where we have multiple lines of evidence here, otoliths providing the age estimates, and bomb radiocarbon confirming and validating the otolith ages and extreme longevity of the blue sucker.”

By comparing the carbon-14 signatures in the otoliths with the known timing of the atmospheric radiocarbon increase, the researchers validated the ages estimated from the growth layers. This independent evidence confirmed that blue suckers can survive for more than a century.

The blue sucker is now the fourth member of the sucker fish family (Catostomidae) found to reach 100 years or older, joining the bigmouth buffalo, smallmouth buffalo, and black buffalo. All four species have had their exceptional longevity documented since 2019, partly through advances in fish aging techniques.

Blue suckers also challenge expectations about how river environments shape animal lifespans. Unlike fish inhabiting relatively calm lakes, they spend their lives in fast-flowing rivers, where maintaining position and navigating currents can require considerable energy. Such environments have often been associated with faster life histories, making the species’ extreme longevity particularly unexpected.

The oldest fish examined had already been alive for decades when many of the dams now shaping the Missouri River system were constructed. Their survival across more than a century of environmental change contrasts with the apparent scarcity of younger generations, raising conservation concerns about whether aging adults are being replaced.

“To put a timeline on some of those older fish: the oldest one hatched around two years after Montana became a state, around the dawn of the automobile, like 20 years before the Titanic sank – it’s just wild,” said Holmquist.

“We start putting it in the context of what the landscape looked like when these fish hatched, and all the changes that have happened since—and they just keep swimming along in the river.”

Reference: “Bomb-radiocarbon validated otoliths reveal 130-year lifespans and declining recruitment for blue sucker Cycleptus elongatus of the Upper Missouri River, Montana, USA” by Alec R. Lackmann, Allen H. Andrews, Luke M. Holmquist, Negar Haghipour, Grant Grisak, Molly A. H. Webb, Mark E. Clark and Zachary R. Shattuck, 18 November 2026, Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-11219-3

Funding for this project was provided by Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks and NorthWestern Energy. The study was also coauthored by Negar Haghipour (ETH Zürich), Grant Grisak (NorthWestern Energy), Molly Webb (USFWS), Mark Clark (UMD – Biology), and Zach Shattuck (MTFWP).

#6277. Lightning could strike the ground more than twice as often by the end of the century

If greenhouse gas emissions stay high, lightning strikes that reach the ground could rise 76% to 140% worldwide by 2100, with even larger increases in Alaska.

Lightning strikes that reach the ground could become 76% to 140% more frequent worldwide by the end of this century, compared with 1995 to 2014, if greenhouse gas emissions stay high.

The numbers are far above previous estimates, and they surprised the researchers who produced them.

During that baseline period, most of Alaska averaged fewer than one strike per square kilometer per year. By the end of the century, the statewide increase could reach 594%.

The study was led by Andreas Krause, an Earth system scientist at the Technical University of Munich.

Lightning has been genuinely hard to forecast, because its two essential ingredients pull in opposite directions under a warming climate.

It starts with heat. Air near the ground warms, becomes buoyant and rises, a process called convection.

That rising air stirs up the much colder atmosphere above it. In the turbulence, tiny ice crystals in the frigid mid-level clouds collide and swap electric charge.

The lighter crystals get carried upward while the heavier ones sink, separating positive from negative and building an electric field between them. When the field grows strong enough, the air breaks down and a bolt fires.

Warmer air near the ground can fuel stronger updrafts, increasing the chances that ice particles collide and build up an electric charge.

We can already see the pattern: lightning peaks in the early afternoon, the hottest part of the day, and the tropics get far more of it than the high latitudes.

Warmer air aloft could mean fewer ice crystals, making it harder for storms to build up the electric charge that produces lightning.

“There is actually quite a large uncertainty about how lightning will respond to climate change,” Krause said. “It’s not quite clear which of these is more important.”

Rather than build the physics from scratch, the team trained a machine learning model on a single year of observations from 2019.

The researchers paired actual lightning records with the weather conditions that produced them: temperature, rainfall, humidity, air pressure, wind speed, and incoming solar radiation.

Then they ran it backwards. Applied to the climate of 1901 to 1920 and again to 1995 to 2014, the model showed cloud-to-ground lightning rising 11% over the 20th century. That works out to roughly 12% more lightning per degree Celsius of warming.

The forward projection is where it gets uncomfortable. Under a high-emissions scenario, that sensitivity nearly triples, to about 30% more lightning per degree.

Compared with the 1995 to 2014 baseline, ground strikes would become 76% to 140% more common by 2100, depending on which climate model you feed in.

For comparison, the highest previous estimates put the figure between 8% and 17% per degree. The gap comes mostly from a different mathematical approach and from this study’s use of a newer, more reliable global lightning dataset.

“I was quite surprised that the projections were so high,” Krause said. “I expected smaller changes.”

The projections apply specifically to cloud-to-ground lightning, the bolts that actually touch down.

Most lightning never reaches the surface, staying within or between clouds, and it does little harm there.

What comes down is another matter. Cloud-to-ground strikes ignite wildfires, damage wind turbines, power lines and offshore oil rigs, and kill several thousand people and hundreds of millions of trees worldwide every year.

The increases won’t be evenly spread. In absolute terms, the biggest rises come where lightning is already thickest: the Amazon, Southeast Asia, and Oceania.

The Amazon projection carries the largest caveat, and the researchers are upfront about it.

Their model learned from the Amazon as it exists today, and that forest may look very different by 2100. Some studies actually predict less tropical lightning in the future, not more.

The biggest proportional changes happen at high latitudes, where lightning is currently rare enough that any increase looks dramatic.

Many of those regions could see strike density more than double. Alaska is the extreme case, somewhere between 116% and 594% above its baseline.

Whether more lightning translates into more danger is a separate question, and it depends on timing.

Krause pointed out that the risk to people may hinge on whether the extra bolts arrive during the early stages of storms.

That’s when someone outdoors is most likely to be caught off guard, before the sky has made its intentions obvious.

The study didn’t examine how forests would cope. In general, Krause said, conifers show more visible damage from a direct strike than broadleaved trees.

Within the tropics, some studies suggest that forests already accustomed to frequent lightning handle it better. That resilience is something he wants to look at next.

“Trees basically evolved to adapt to the local lightning frequency,” Krause said. “But are there any species that are particularly tolerant of lightning strikes and more likely to survive them? There’s not much information out there.”

The study is published in the journal Earth’s Future.
